title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Count valence electrons first (S and O are both group 16). If a double bond can sit on either S–O side, you have resonance. Then count electron groups on S, including its lone pair.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Count the electrons around the central atom in each. Fewer than 8 is incomplete; more than 8 is expanded. An odd total of valence electrons means a radical.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Start with valence electrons: K is in group 1, O in group 16. How many electrons does O need, and how many K atoms does it take to supply them?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Look for the ion that decides: does the formula contain OH<sup>−</sup> (base), the oxide ion O<sup>2−</sup> with a metal (metal oxide), or neither (salt)?
why: LiOH contains the hydroxide ion, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is a metal with the oxide ion, and CaCO<sub>3</sub> is a metal cation with a polyatomic anion that is neither OH<sup>−</sup> nor O<sup>2−</sup>.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: To carry a current, charged particles must be able to move. Ask where the ions are free to move: in the crystal lattice or in water?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Al is in group 13 and F in group 17. Each F needs only one electron, so do not give all of Al's electrons to one F. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use the group number: an atom usually forms as many bonds as the electrons it needs to reach an octet, and its leftover valence electrons pair up as lone pairs.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Think about how many pairs are shared. The more shared pairs between two atoms, the shorter and stronger the bond.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Count O<sub>2</sub>'s valence electrons, then try a single bond. Does each O end up with 8 electrons using only that many?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Add the group-number valence electrons of every atom. For an ion, add one electron per negative charge and subtract one per positive charge.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Count valence electrons, put S in the center (H is never central), connect with single bonds, then place what is left as lone pairs. Compare with water.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Count 10 electrons and connect H–C–N with single bonds. Check octets: if C is short, move lone pairs from N into the C–N bond.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Let the bond counts build the skeleton: which atom bonds to the most things? After single bonds and lone pairs, check octets and erase a lone pair to make a double bond where needed.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Count the electrons, build the skeleton from the formula with single bonds, and place lone pairs. Which atoms are short of their usual bond counts?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Count valence electrons for an ion: add one for the 1− charge. Put N in the center, and remember the brackets and the charge outside.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: For each, draw the Lewis structure and count electron groups on the central atom (a multiple bond counts as one group). Then ask whether any groups are lone pairs.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Count how many of the 4 groups are bonds and how many are lone pairs. The shape names only where the atoms are.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Look at one carbon at a time. Count its electron groups, remembering that the C=C double bond counts as one group.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Count groups on N (bonds plus lone pairs) and picture that many balloons. Pop the lone-pair balloon without moving the others. Wedges come toward you; dashes go away.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Find ΔEN for each bond with the yellow-sheet electronegativities (larger minus smaller). A bigger difference means a more polar bond.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: First get the shape from the Lewis structure (does P have a lone pair?). Then use SNAP: do the polar bonds cancel?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Both have polar bonds, so decide by shape. Which shape lets three equal bond dipoles cancel, and which has a lone pair on the central atom?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Draw an arrow only for each polar bond (ΔEN above 0.4). Follow the arrows like driving directions: if you end up back where you started, they cancel.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: (a) Count electron groups around each carbon separately. (b) Which bond has a large ΔEN, and is anything on the other side to cancel it? Polar mixes with polar.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Mass of N in one mole: subscript × atomic mass (count every N in the formula). Then part ÷ whole × 100%.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Use one mole: there is one C in CO<sub>2</sub>. Divide the mass of C by the molar mass and multiply by 100%.
why: Mass percent is the element's mass in one mole (1 × 12.011 g of C) divided by the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub>, times 100%.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Part ÷ whole × 100%, where the whole is the sample mass. The oxygen mass is whatever is left after the copper.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Find %Cu from the formula (two Cu per Cu<sub>2</sub>S), then use it as a conversion factor: g Cu per 100 g Cu<sub>2</sub>S.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Compute the measured %Cl from the sample, then the %Cl expected from the formula NaCl. Do they agree?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Divide every subscript by the largest number that divides all of them. If they cannot be reduced, the formula is already empirical.
why: Each empirical formula is the molecular formula divided by the largest common factor of its subscripts (2, 2, 6 and 2), giving the simplest whole-number ratio.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Assume 100 g so percents become grams, convert to moles (the goal is the mole), and divide by the smallest. Then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Multiply every subscript by n.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: (a) The data are already in moles: divide each by the smallest. (b) Compare the given molar mass with the empirical formula mass to find n.

title: Problem 6.1
hint: Calcium is in group 2 and fluorine in group 17. How many electrons must Ca lose, and how many can one F accept? Metals lose, nonmetals gain.

title: Problem 6.2
hint: (a) Use group numbers. (b) Find the smallest number both 3 (lost per Al) and 2 (gained per O) divide into. (c) Write the formula from those counts.

title: Problem 6.3
hint: Look for the ions: OH<sup>−</sup> means base; a metal with O<sup>2−</sup> means metal oxide; other ion pairs (including NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) mean salt; two nonmetals with no ions means not ionic.

title: Problem 6.4
hint: A current needs charged particles that can move. Which choice has ions, and are they free to move?

title: Problem 6.5
hint: (a) Multiply each ion's charge by how many there are, then add. (b) Compare the charges of F<sup>−</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup>. (c) Count each polyatomic ion as one ion.

title: Problem 6.6
hint: Count electrons: Mg has 12 and O has 8. How many does each ion have after losing or gaining 2? Which noble gas has that many?

title: Problem 6.7
hint: Count N<sub>2</sub>'s valence electrons, then count the electrons each choice uses. Never add electrons to complete octets; HONC says N forms 3 bonds.

title: Problem 6.8
hint: (a) Add group-number electrons. (b) The three single bonds use some; the rest go as lone pairs. (c) Count electrons around each O and each H.

title: Problem 6.9
hint: Count the shared electron pairs in each bond. Does sharing more pairs hold the two carbons closer together or farther apart?

title: Problem 6.10
hint: For each molecule, count valence electrons, connect the atoms, and place the rest as lone pairs. Remember H gets a duet, not an octet.

title: Problem 6.11
hint: Use HONC (carbon forms 4 bonds). In which molecule can't every atom reach its usual bond count with single bonds alone?

title: Problem 6.12
hint: Use the group number: each bond to H gives the element one more electron toward an octet. Leftover valence electrons pair up as lone pairs.

title: Problem 6.13
hint: Add the group-number valence electrons of every atom. For an ion, add one per negative charge and subtract one per positive charge.

title: Problem 6.14
hint: Check each choice: total electrons used must be 14, carbon makes 4 bonds (HONC), Cl usually 1, and no atom other than H has more or less than 8.

title: Problem 6.15
hint: (a) Add valence electrons. (b) Which atom appears once and is less electronegative? (c) Connect with single bonds, fill outer atoms first, and put any leftovers on the center.

title: Problem 6.16
hint: Count each ion's electrons (adjust for the charge), place bonds and lone pairs, then put the structure in brackets with the charge outside.

title: Problem 6.17
hint: (a) Read the formula as a CH<sub>3</sub> group joined to an OH group. (b) Count electrons and subtract the bonding pairs. (c) How many bonds can H form?

title: Problem 6.18
hint: Count the electrons each description uses (it must be 12) and check that every carbon has 4 bonds and 8 electrons.

title: Problem 6.19
hint: (a) Which atoms can form only one bond? (b) Add group-number electrons. (c) Connect with single bonds, then fill octets with lone pairs.

title: Problem 6.20
hint: Draw each Lewis structure first, then count groups on the central atom only (any bond is one group; each lone pair is one group). Pop the lone pairs to name the shape.

title: Problem 6.21
hint: Count electron groups on O, including lone pairs. Then name the shape from the atoms only, not from the flat Lewis drawing.

title: Problem 6.22
hint: A double bond counts as one electron group, and only lone pairs on the central atom count. How many groups does carbon have?

title: Problem 6.23
hint: Treat each center separately. Count bonds and lone pairs on C, then on O, and pop the lone pairs to name each shape.

title: Problem 6.24
hint: (a) Count valence electrons and compare with the bonds drawn. (b) Count groups on each carbon (the triple bond is one group). (c) Put the two centers together.

title: Problem 6.25
hint: For each molecule or ion, count electron groups and lone pairs on the central atom. The same counts give the same shape, whatever the charge.

title: Problem 6.26
hint: The holes play the role of electron groups. (a) What fills a group if no atom does? (b) Name the shape by the atoms only. (c) Count N's bonds.

title: Problem 6.27
hint: For each bond, subtract the smaller electronegativity from the larger and compare with the cutoffs: 0–0.4, above 0.4–2.0, above 2.0. The more electronegative atom is δ−.

title: Problem 6.28
hint: Compute ΔEN for each bond (larger minus smaller). The largest difference is the most polar bond.

title: Problem 6.29
hint: Compute ΔEN for each pair and compare with the cutoff: above 2.0 is ionic. Use only the numbers, not the metal–nonmetal rule.

title: Problem 6.30
hint: Each has a basic shape with no lone pairs on carbon, so check the outer atoms (SNAP). Which molecule has outer atoms that are not all the same?

title: Problem 6.31
hint: Find ΔEN to classify the bond. Then decide which atom pulls the shared pair closer, which end gets δ−, and which way the dipole arrow points.

title: Problem 6.32
hint: (a) For each, check bond polarity and then shape. (b) What is the shape of CO<sub>2</sub>, and which way do its two bond dipoles point?

title: Problem 6.33
hint: (a) Compute ΔEN. (b) Count groups on N, including the lone pair. (c) Use SNAP: is the shape symmetrical?

title: Problem 6.34
hint: (a) The 2 outside the parentheses doubles everything inside: count each atom, then add. (b) For each element, mass in one mole ÷ molar mass × 100%.

title: Problem 6.35
hint: For each, find the mass of O in one mole and the molar mass, then part ÷ whole. More O atoms alone does not guarantee the highest percent.

title: Problem 6.36
hint: (a) Subtract the crucible mass each time; oxygen is product minus magnesium. (b) Part ÷ whole × 100%, where the whole is the product.

title: Problem 6.37
hint: (a) Molar mass of KI, then mass of I ÷ molar mass × 100%. (b) Use the percent as a conversion factor: mg I per 100 mg KI.

title: Problem 6.38
hint: Find the phosphate and hydroxide masses first, then multiply by their counts. Percent = mass of the element in one mole ÷ molar mass × 100%.

title: Problem 6.39
hint: Think about the law of constant composition. Does the percent of an element in a pure compound depend on sample size or source?

title: Problem 6.40
hint: Divide each set of subscripts by the largest number that divides all of them, then compare the reduced formulas in each pair.

title: Problem 6.41
hint: Assume 100 g, so each percent becomes grams. Convert to moles (the goal is the mole) and divide by the smallest. Then find n from the molar mass.

title: Problem 6.42
hint: Assume 100 g, convert to moles, and divide by the smaller. If a ratio ends in .5, do not round: multiply both by 2. Then find n.

title: Problem 6.43
hint: Assume 100 g, convert to moles, and divide by the smaller. A ratio like 2.67 is a fraction in thirds: find the multiplier that makes it whole.

title: Problem 6.44
hint: (a) Oxygen is product mass minus Mg mass. Convert both to moles and divide by the smaller. (b) Do the charges of Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup> allow that ratio?

title: Problem 6.45
hint: Find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Which choice is (CH<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>n</sub>?

title: Problem 6.46
hint: Water lost = hydrate mass minus anhydrous mass. Convert both masses to moles, then x = mol H<sub>2</sub>O ÷ mol MgSO<sub>4</sub>.

title: Problem 6.47
hint: Find the water lost, then convert both the water and the CaSO<sub>4</sub> to moles. Compare moles, not grams, with water on top.

title: Problem 6.48
hint: (a) Use the prefix for the number of F. (b) Add group-number electrons. (c) N is less electronegative, so it is central. (d) Count groups on N. (e) Use SNAP.

title: Problem 6.49
hint: (a) Two nonmetals: use prefixes. (b) Count 14 electrons. (c) Molar mass, then mass of Si ÷ molar mass × 100%. (d) Compare ΔEN with the cutoffs.

title: Problem 6.50
hint: Metal plus nonmetal is ionic; two nonmetals is molecular. Compute ΔEN for each bond, then for the molecular ones count groups on the center and apply SNAP.

title: Problem 6.51
hint: Count 15 electrons into orbitals in order. The valence electrons are the outermost s and p. How many more does P need to match the next noble gas?

title: Problem 6.52
hint: (a) Use the green sheet for nitrate. (b) Which pieces are held by attraction between ions, and which by shared electrons? (c) Part ÷ whole. (d) Find moles first; the goal is the mole.

title: Problem 6.53
hint: Use the usual bond counts: which atom forms the most bonds? Draw the structure, then count electron groups (including lone pairs) on that atom.

title: Problem 6.54
hint: A molecule is polar if its bond arrows do not cancel. For each, check which bonds are polar (ΔEN above 0.4) and whether the outer atoms are all the same.

title: Problem 6.55
hint: (a) Treat each carbon and the oxygen as separate centers and count their groups. (b) Are the two C–O dipoles pointing in opposite directions? (c) Compare the two structures.

title: Problem 6.56
hint: Find the measured %Fe from the sample, then the %Fe expected from each formula. A pure compound must match its formula's percent.

title: Problem 6.57
hint: (a) Count the N atoms (the 2 outside the parentheses doubles NH<sub>2</sub>), find the molar mass, then part ÷ whole. (b) Use the percent as kg N per 100 kg urea.

title: Problem 6.58
hint: The data are already in moles: divide by the smallest to get the empirical formula, then n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

title: Problem 6.59
hint: (a) Add group-number electrons. (b) Try placing the double bond on each side of the central O. (c) Count groups on the central O. (d) Think about the resonance hybrid.

title: Problem 6.60
hint: (a) Add group-number electrons. (b) Is the total odd or even? Bonds and lone pairs hold electrons in pairs. (c) What do we call a molecule with an unpaired electron?

title: Problem 6.61
hint: (a) Add one electron for the 1− charge. (b) How many different O atoms could hold the double bond? (c) Count groups on N; it has no lone pairs.
